region.en: The age of the ancients (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 古之世（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 6, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 6

summary.en: Zhuangzi's portrait of the pure men of old: they acted without calculation, could scale heights without fear, enter water without becoming wet, fire without feeling hot; they slept without dreams, breathed from their uttermost depths, and did not love life nor hate death — quickly come, quickly go — playing their allotted parts and waiting patiently for the end.
summary.zh: 古之真人：不逆寡，不雄成，不謨士；登高不慄，入水不濡，入火不熱；其寢不夢，其覺無憂，其息深深；不知說生，不知惡死——翛然而往，翛然而來而已矣。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the archetypal zhenren portrait that later Daoist hagiography made concrete. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: But what is a pure man?--The pure men of old acted without calculation, not seeking to secure results. They laid no plans. Therefore, failing, they had no cause for regret; succeeding, no cause for congratulation. And thus they could scale heights without fear; enter water without becoming wet; fire, without feeling hot. So far had their wisdom advanced towards TAO.

The pure men of old slept without dreams, and waked without anxiety. They ate without discrimination, breathing deep breaths. For pure men draw breath from their uttermost depths; the vulgar only from their throats. The pure men of old did not know what it was to love life or to hate death. They did not rejoice in birth, nor strive to put off dissolution. Quickly come, and quickly go;--no more. They did not forget whence it was they had sprung, neither did they seek to hasten their return thither. Cheerfully they played their allotted parts, waiting patiently for the end.

title.en: Before Heaven and Earth: The Transmission of the Tao (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 夫道，有情有信，無為無形（莊子）

region.en: Mount T'ai and the cosmic stations (symbolic pin: Mount T'ai, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 泰山與諸天寰宇（象徵定位：山東泰山）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 6, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 6

summary.en: The genealogy of the Tao itself: before heaven and earth were, TAO was; the Great Bear obtained it and never erred from its course; K'an P'i established the K'un-lun mountains; the Yellow Emperor soared on the clouds to heaven; Yü Ch'iang fixed himself at the North Pole; Hsi Wang Mu settled at Shao Kuang; P'êng Tsu lived from Shun to the Five Princes; and Fu Yüeh, charioted upon one constellation, was enrolled among the stars.
summary.zh: 夫道，有情有信，無為無形；可得而不可見；自本自根，未有天地，自古以固存。狶韋氏得之以挈天地；堪坏得之以襲崑崙；馮夷得之以遊大川；肩吾得之以處太山；黃帝得之以登雲天；西王母得之坐乎少廣；彭祖得之，上及有虞，下及五伯；傅說得之，乘東維騎箕尾而比於列星。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); a priority Creation & Cosmology narrative — the scriptural charter for Taoist cosmogony and for the deification of sages.

passages.text: TAO has its laws, and its evidences. It is devoid both of action and of form. It may be transmitted, but cannot be received. It may be obtained, but cannot be seen. Before heaven and earth were, TAO was. It has existed without change from all time. Spiritual beings drew their spirituality therefrom, while the universe became what we can see it now. To TAO, the zenith is not high, nor the nadir low; no point in time is long ago, nor by lapse of ages has it grown old.

Hsi Wei obtained TAO, and so set the universe in order. Fu Hsi obtained it, and was able to establish eternal principles. The Great Bear obtained it, and has never erred from its course. The sun and moon obtained it, and have never ceased to revolve. K'an P'i obtained it, and established the K'un-lun mountains. P'ing I obtained it, and rules over the streams. Chien Wu obtained it, and dwells on Mount T'ai.

The Yellow Emperor obtained it, and soared upon the clouds to heaven. Chuan Hsü obtained it, and dwells in the Dark Palace. Yü Ch'iang obtained it, and fixed himself at the North Pole. Hsi Wang Mu obtained it, and settled at Shao Kuang; since when, no one knows; until when, no one knows either. P'êng Tsu obtained it, and lived from the time of Shun until the time of the Five Princes. Fu Yüeh obtained it, and as the Minister of Wu Ting got the empire under his control. And now, charioted upon one constellation and drawn by another, he has been enrolled among the stars of heaven.

title.en: Nü Yü Teaches the Tao in Nine Days (Zhuangzi)

region.en: The hermit's plot (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 隱者之圃（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 6, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 6

summary.en: Nan Po Tzŭ K'uei asks the aged Nü Yü why his countenance is like a child's; she answers that she has learnt the Tao. In three days Pu Liang I ceased to see the sublunary state; in seven more the external world; in nine he became unconscious of his own existence — first etherealised, then possessed of perfect wisdom, then without past or present, finally able to enter where life and death are no more.
summary.zh: 南伯子葵問乎女偊：子之年長矣，而色若孺子，何也？曰：吾聞道矣——三日而後能外天下；七日而後能外物；九日而後能外生；而後朝徹、見獨，而後能無古今；而後能入於不死不生。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the three-stage inner-cultivation scheme is the ancestor of later Daoist meditation grades. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: "I fear not," said Nü Yü. "You are not the sort of man. There was Pu Liang I. He had all the qualifications of a sage, but not TAO. Now I had Tao, though none of the qualifications. But do you imagine that much as I wished it I was able to teach TAO to him so that he should be a perfect sage? Had it been so, then to teach TAO to one who has the qualifications of a sage would be an easy matter. No, Sir. I imparted as though withholding; and in three days, for him, this sublunary state had ceased to exist.

When he had attained to this, I withheld again; and in seven days more, for him, the external world had ceased to be. And so again for another nine days, when he became unconscious of his own existence. He became first etherealised, next possessed of perfect wisdom, then without past or present, and finally able to enter there where life and death are no more,--where killing does not take away life, nor does prolongation of life add to the duration of existence.

"And how did you manage to get hold of all this?" asked Nan Po Tzŭ K'uei. "I got it from books," replied Nü Yü; "and the books got it from learning, and learning from investigation, and investigation from cö-ordination, and cö-ordination from application, and application from desire to know, and desire to know from the unknown, and the unknown from the great void, and the great void from infinity!"

title.en: Tzŭ Yü's Illness: Cock, Cross-bow, and Chariot (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 子輿有病，曲僂發背（莊子）

region.en: The four friends' meeting-place (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 四子相與之地（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 6, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 6

summary.en: Four friends pledge that whoever can make Inaction the head, Life the backbone, and Death the tail of his existence shall be their friend. Tzŭ Yü falls ill, doubled up and deranged, and greets the change without fear: his left shoulder will become a cock to herald the morn, his right a cross-bow, his buttocks wheels with his soul for a horse — I obtained life because it was my time; I part with it in accordance with the same law.
summary.zh: 四人相與語曰：孰能以無為首，以生為脊，以死為尻？子輿有病，子祀往問；子輿曰：亡，予何惡——浸假而化予之左臂以為雞，右臂以為彈，尻以為輪，以神為馬，予因乘之。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Four men were conversing together, when the following resolution was suggested:--"Whosoever can make Inaction the head, Life the backbone, and Death the tail, of his existence,--that man shall be admitted to friendship with us." The four looked at each other and smiled; and tacitly accepting the conditions, became friends forthwith. By-and-by, one of them, named Tzŭ Yü, fell ill, and another, Tzŭ Ssŭ, went to see him. "Verily God is great!" said the sick man. "See how he has doubled me up. My back is so hunched that my viscera are at the top of my body. My cheeks are level with my navel. My shoulders are higher than my neck. My hair grows up towards the sky. The whole economy of my organism is deranged. Nevertheless, my mental equilibrium is not disturbed."

"I am not [afraid]," replied Tzŭ Yü. "What have I to fear? Ere long I shall be decomposed. My left shoulder will become a cock, and I shall herald the approach of morn. My right shoulder will become a cross-bow, and I shall be able to get broiled duck. My buttocks will become wheels; and with my soul for a horse, I shall be able to ride in my own chariot. I obtained life because it was my time: I am now parting with it in accordance with the same law. Content with the natural sequence of these states, joy and sorrow touch me not. I am simply, as the ancients expressed it, hanging in the air, unable to cut myself down, bound with the trammels of material existence. But man has ever given way before God: why, then, should I be afraid?"

title.zh: 子來臨終：大冶鑄金（莊子）

region.en: The four friends' home (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 四子之家（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 6, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 6

summary.en: Tzŭ Lai lies gasping while his family weeps; Tzŭ Li drives them off and asks what God will make of him next — a rat's liver or a snake's shoulders. Tzŭ Lai answers that Nature is a man's parents: the universe is the smelting-pot and God the caster, and were he to cry 'Make of me a man!' he would be rejected as uncanny. I shall go whithersoever I am sent, as a man wakes from a dreamless sleep.
summary.zh: 子來有病，喘喘然將死；子犁往問，斥其妻子：無怛化！彼且以造化為父母——今一以天地為大爐，以造化為大冶，惡乎往而不可哉！

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the Creator-as-smelter image grounds the Taoist death-and-transformation cluster. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: By-and-by, another of the four, named Tzŭ Lai, fell ill, and lay gasping for breath, while his family stood weeping around. The fourth friend, Tzŭ Li, went to see him. "Chut!" cried he to the wife and children; "begone! you balk his decomposition." Then, leaning against the door, he said, "Verily, God is great! I wonder what he will make of you now. I wonder whither you will be sent. Do you think he will make you into a rat's liver or into the shoulders of a snake?"

"A son," answered Tzŭ Lai, "must go whithersoever his parents bid him. Nature is no other than a man's parents. If she bid me die quickly, and I demur, then I am an unfilial son. She can do me no wrong. TAO gives me this form, this toil in manhood, this repose in old age, this rest in death. And surely that which is such a kind arbiter of my life is the best arbiter of my death.

"Suppose that the boiling metal in a smelting-pot were to bubble up and say, 'Make of me an Excalibur;' I think the caster would reject that metal as uncanny. And if a sinner like myself were to say to God, 'Make of me a man, make of me a man;' I think he too would reject me as uncanny. The universe is the smelting-pot, and God is the caster. I shall go whithersoever I am sent, to wake unconscious of the past, as a man wakes from a dreamless sleep."

title.en: The Song at Tzŭ Sang Hu's Corpse (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 子桑戶死，孟子反琴曲（莊子）

region.en: The mourners' hall (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 吊喪之堂（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 6, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 6

summary.en: Three friends resolve to mount to heaven, roaming through the clouds beyond the limits of space. When Tzŭ Sang Hu dies, his two friends sing beside the corpse: 'Thou hast already returned to thy God, while we still remain here as men, alas!' Tzŭ Kung protests the breach of decorum; Confucius explains that these men look on life as a huge tumour from which death sets them free — for fishes are born in water, and man is born in TAO.
summary.zh: 子桑戶、孟子反、子琴張三人相與友；桑戶死，未葬，二子臨尸而歌：嗟來桑戶乎！而已反其真，而我猶為人猗！孔子曰：彼遊方之外者也，而丘遊方之內者也；魚相忘乎江湖，人相忘乎道術。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Tzŭ Sang Hu, Mêng Tzŭ Fan, and Tzŭ Ch'in Chang, were conversing together, when it was asked, "Who can be, and yet not be? Who can do, and yet not do? Who can mount to heaven, and roaming through the clouds, pass beyond the limits of space, oblivious of existence, for ever and ever without end?" The three looked at each other and smiled; and as neither had any misgivings, they became friends accordingly. Shortly afterwards Tzŭ Sang Hu died; whereupon Confucius sent Tzŭ Kung to take part in the mourning. But Tzŭ Kung found that one had composed a song which the other was accompanying on the lute, as follows:--"Ah! Wilt thou come back to us, Sang Hu? Ah! Wilt thou come back to us, Sang Hu? Thou hast already returned to thy God, While we still remain here as men,--alas!"

"These men," replied Confucius, "travel beyond the rule of life. I travel within it. Consequently, our paths do not meet; and I was wrong in sending you to mourn. They consider themselves as one with God, recognising no distinctions between human and divine. They look on life as a huge tumour from which death sets them free. All the same they know not where they were before birth, nor where they will be after death. Though admitting different elements, they take their stand upon the unity of all things. ... They stroll beyond the dust and dirt of mortality, to wander in the realms of inaction. How should such men trouble themselves with the conventionalities of this world, or care what people may think of them?"

"Fishes," replied Confucius, "are born in water. Man is born in TAO. If fishes get ponds to live in, they thrive. If man gets TAO to live in, he may live his life in peace. Hence the saying, 'All that a fish wants is water; all that a man wants is TAO.'"

title.en: Yen Hui Gets Rid of Everything (Zhuangzi)

region.en: The court of Lu (Qufu, Shandong, China)

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 6, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 6

summary.en: Yen Hui reports his progress three times to Confucius: first getting rid of charity and duty, then of ceremonial and music, finally of everything — I have freed myself from my body, discarded my reasoning powers, and become one with the Infinite. Confucius eagerly grants that if he has become one there can be no room for bias, and asks to follow in his steps.
summary.zh: 顏回曰：回益矣——忘仁義矣，忘禮樂矣，墮肢體，黜聰明，離形去知，同於大通，此謂坐忘。仲尼曰：同則無好也，化則無常也，而果其賢乎，丘也請從而後也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the 'sitting-and-forgetting' (zuowang) charter for Daoist meditation. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: "I am getting on," observed Yen Hui to Confucius. "How so?" asked the latter. "I have got rid of charity and duty," replied the former. "Very good," replied Confucius, "but not perfect." Another day Yen Hui met Confucius and said, "I am getting on." "How so?" asked Confucius. "I have got rid of ceremonial and music," answered Yen Hui. "Very good," said Confucius, "but not perfect."

On a third occasion Yen Hui met Confucius and said, "I am getting on." "How so?" asked the Sage. "I have got rid of everything," replied Yen Hui. "Got rid of everything!" said Confucius eagerly. "What do you mean by that?" "I have freed myself from my body," answered Yen Hui. "I have discarded my reasoning powers. And by thus getting rid of body and mind, I have become ONE with the Infinite. This is what I mean by getting rid of everything." "If you have become ONE," cried Confucius, "there can be no room for bias. If you have passed into space, you are indeed without beginning or end. And if you have really attained to this, I trust to be allowed to follow in your steps."
